authors: Fernández-Juricic E, O'Rourke C, Pitlik T
title: Visual coverage and scanning behavior in two corvid species: American crow and Western scrub jay
why: Measures binocular field width, blind area, eye movement amplitude and head-movement rate on the ground for the American crow (and a jay for the genus-level blue jay comparison).

authors: Cantlay JC, Portugal SJ, Martin GR
title: Visual fields, foraging and collision vulnerability in gulls (Laridae)
why: Binocular field, blind area and monocular fields of herring and lesser black-backed gulls (genus Larus) for the ring-billed gull.

authors: Fernández-Juricic E, Baumhardt PE, Tyrrell LP, Elmore A, DeLiberto ST, Werner SJ
title: Vision in an abundant North American bird: The Red-winged Blackbird
why: Measures visual coverage, binocular field, acuity, foveae and UV/colour vision in the red-winged blackbird itself.
get: open access (Auk/Ornithology is open access; also https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/icwdm_usdanwrc/2280)

authors: Rojas LM, McNeil R, Cabana T, Lachapelle P
title: Diurnal and nocturnal visual function in two tactile foraging waterbirds: the American White Ibis and the Black Skimmer
why: Rod and cone density, ganglion cell density and ERG sensitivity in the American white ibis itself (no DOI printed on the PDF; cite by Condor 99:191-200).

authors: Rojas LM, McNeil R, Cabana T, Lachapelle P
title: Behavioral, morphological and physiological correlates of diurnal and nocturnal vision in selected wading bird species
why: ERG and retinal histology across herons, egrets, an ibis and a spoonbill; would give rod:cone and night-vision rows for great egret (genus-level via other egrets) and white ibis.

authors: Cronin T, Kinloch M, Olsen GH
title: Head-bobbing behavior in foraging Whooping Cranes
why: Head-bob fixation timing in a walking crane; closest measured Grus for the sandhill crane head-movement row.

authors: Cantlay JC, Martin GR, McClelland SC, Potier S, O'Brien MF, Fernández-Juricic E, Bond AL, Portugal SJ
title: Binocular vision and foraging in ducks, geese and swans (Anatidae)
journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society B 290: 20231213
why: Binocular field width and shape for 39 Anatidae including Anas platyrhynchos (mallard) and A. rubripes; settles mallard and dabbling-duck binocular overlap.

authors: Martin GR, Katzir G
title: Visual fields and eye movements in herons (Ardeidae)
why: Binocular field, blind area and eye movement of cattle egret, squacco and reef herons; the nearest measured egrets for the great egret.

authors: Martin GR, White CR, Butler PJ
title: Vision and the foraging technique of Great Cormorants Phalacrocorax carbo: pursuit or close-quarter foraging?
why: Visual field and eye movement of a cormorant, the closest relative measured to the anhinga (a darter that spears fish).

authors: Martin GR, Katzir G
title: Visual fields, foraging and binocularity in birds
journal: Proceedings of the 22nd International Ornithological Congress, Durban (Adams NJ, Slotow RH, eds), pp. 2711-2728
why: Cross-species review of visual-field types and binocular width (owls, herons, mallard, eagle) that a display panel on binocular overlap could cite.

authors: Martin GR
title: What is binocular vision for? A birds' eye view
why: Review of binocular field widths across bird orders (owls, raptors, herons, ducks) that a museum panel on overlap could quote.

authors: Lind O, Mitkus M, Olsson P, Kelber A
title: Ultraviolet vision in birds: the importance of transparent eye media
journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society B 281: 20132209
why: Ocular media UV transmission across many bird species; settles whether violet- versus UV-type cones can pass UV in the eye for species with SWS1 sequences.

authors: Potier S, Mitkus M, Kelber A
title: High resolution of colour vision, but low contrast sensitivity in a diurnal raptor
journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society B 285: 20181036
why: Behavioural colour and contrast thresholds in a diurnal raptor; closest measured values for red-shouldered hawk, osprey, eagle contrast rows.

authors: Mitkus M, Potier S, Martin GR, Duriez O, Kelber A
title: Raptor Vision
why: Review of raptor foveae, acuity, visual fields and UV/colour vision with species tables; panel-level background for eagle, osprey, hawk, kite, owl.

authors: Blary C, Duriez O, Bonadonna F, Mitkus M, Caro S, Besnard A, Potier S
title: Low achromatic contrast sensitivity in birds: a common attribute shared by most phylogenetic orders
why: Contrast sensitivity across many bird orders; could give a contrast row for several of the listed taxa by order.

authors: Ault SJ
title: Electroretinograms and retinal structure of the eastern screech owl (Otus asio) and great horned owl (Bubo virginianus)
why: Retinal structure and ERG sensitivity in the eastern screech owl and great horned owl themselves (no DOI; open access via SORA PDF).

authors: Braekevelt CR
title: Fine structure of the retinal photoreceptors of the great horned owl (Bubo virginianus)
why: Gives rod:single cone:double cone ratio of about 30:1:2 and a colourless 3 micron oil droplet in the great horned owl.

authors: Ault SJ, House EW
title: Electroretinographic responses of the great horned owl Bubo virginianus
why: ERG spectral and flicker responses in the great horned owl; flicker-related and sensitivity rows (volume and pages not on the BHL page; check the PDF).

authors: Bowmaker JK, Wilkie SE, Hunt DM
title: Photoreceptors and molecular genetics of visual pigments
journal: Proceedings of the 22nd International Ornithological Congress, Durban (Adams NJ, Slotow RH, eds)
why: Review of avian cone types and oil droplets, naming the mallard among measured species; background for the violet or UV cone question in ducks.

authors: Fernández-Juricic E, Ojeda A, Deisher M, Burry B, Baumhardt P, Stark A, Elmore AG, Ensminger AL
title: Do male and female cowbirds see their world differently? Implications for sex differences in the sensory system of an avian brood parasite
why: Fovea position, single and double cone densities and head-movement rate in an icterid (brown-headed cowbird), the nearest measured relative of grackle and blackbird apart from the red-winged blackbird itself.

authors: Baumhardt PE, Moore BA, Doppler M, Fernández-Juricic E
title: Do American goldfinches see their world like passive prey foragers? A study on visual fields, retinal topography, and sensitivity of photoreceptors
why: Full visual-system profile (binocular field 46 deg, single fovea, UV cone peak near 399 nm) of a small North American passerine; stand-in context for cardinal and palm warbler (finch relatives).

authors: Moore BA
title: A multidimensional approach to comparative avian visual systems (PhD dissertation, Purdue University)
why: Compares 29 North American species across 14 families (visual fields, retinal specialisation, head and eye movement); species list is not on the abstract page so read the thesis to see whether blue jay, cardinal, crow, grackle, mockingbird are in it.

authors: Gondo M, Ando H
title: Comparative and histophysiological study of oil droplets in the avian retina
journal: Kobe Journal of the Medical Sciences 41(4): 127-139
why: Oil droplet colours across 30 species including scarlet ibis (same genus as white ibis), Pekin duck (domestic mallard), herring and black-headed gulls, little egret, night heron, jungle crow, magpie, Ural owl.

authors: Navarro-Sempere A, García M, Cobo R, Pascual-García S, Segovia Y
title: A comprehensive microscopy analysis of the retina of Larus audouinii (Payraudeau, 1826): environmental and ecological insights
why: Cone:rod ratios (about 3:1 to 5:1 centrally) and an acute-vision region in a Larus gull; genus-level source for ring-billed gull photoreceptor rows.

authors: Victory N, Segovia Y, García M
title: Foveal shape, ultrastructure and photoreceptor composition in yellow-legged gull, Larus michahellis (Naumann, 1840)
why: Fovea shape and cone types in a Larus gull; closest fovea and photoreceptor source for the ring-billed gull.
get: open access repository copy (https://hdl.handle.net/10045/113216) or journal via library

authors: Abid SA, Haba MK
title: A histological study of the black-winged kite's retina (Elanus caeruleus, Desfontaines, 1789)
why: Deep and shallow fovea and cone:rod arrangement in a kite; background only for snail kite (different genus, no DOI on page).

authors: Garcés Torres RS, Carter RT, Gafen HB, Liu C-C, Lewin AC, MacLean RA
title: Longitudinal intraocular pressure measurements in whooping cranes (Grus americana) and Mississippi sandhill cranes (Grus canadensis pulla)
why: Eye measurements in a sandhill crane subspecies; related ocular-parameter paper in the same group (title taken from EBSCO link; confirm DOI before download).

authors: Lafitte A, Sordello R, Legrand M, Nicolas V, Obein G, Reyjol Y
title: A flashing light may not be that flashy: a systematic review on critical fusion frequencies
why: Table of 200 critical fusion frequency values for 156 species; would show which of the listed birds (crow, gull, duck, raptors, owls) have a measured value and what it is.

authors: Healy K, McNally L, Ruxton GD, Cooper N, Jackson AL
title: Metabolic rate and body size are linked with perception of temporal information
why: Scaling of flicker fusion with body size and metabolic rate across vertebrates, with a species table; lets a flicker row for an unmeasured bird be estimated from body mass.

authors: Boström JE, Dimitrova M, Canton C, Håstad O, Qvarnström A, Ödeen A
title: Ultra-rapid vision in birds
why: Flicker fusion above 100 Hz in three small wild passerines; supports a passerine flicker row for cardinal, warbler, mockingbird by family.

authors: Lisney TJ, Iwaniuk AN, Bandet MV, Wylie DR
title: Eye shape and retinal topography in owls (Aves: Strigiformes)
why: Eye shape, ganglion cell density, visual streak and fovea measured in great horned owl and barred owl themselves (eastern screech owl not included).

authors: Brooke MdeL, Hanley S, Laughlin SB
title: The scaling of eye size with body mass in birds
journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society B 266
why: Eye mass versus body mass across 104 families (raptors and owls proportionally large); lets an eye-size row be estimated for eagle, osprey, owls, crow, gull (DOI not on the page; PMC1689681).

authors: Lisney TJ, Stecyk K, Kolominsky J, Schmidt BK, Corfield JR, Iwaniuk AN, Wylie DR
title: Ecomorphology of eye shape and retinal topography in waterfowl (Aves: Anseriformes) with different feeding modes
why: Eye shape and ganglion cell topography for dabbling and diving ducks, geese and swans; check whether mallard is among the species; no DOI on the repository page, so find it from the journal record.

authors: O'Rourke CT, Pitlik T, Hoover MM, Fernández-Juricic E
title: Hawk Eyes II: diurnal raptors differ in head movement strategies when scanning from perches
why: Head-movement rate and pause length in red-tailed hawk (same genus as red-shouldered hawk), Cooper's hawk and kestrel.

authors: O'Rourke CT, Hall MI, Pitlik T, Fernández-Juricic E
title: Hawk Eyes I: diurnal raptors differ in visual fields and degree of eye movement
why: Visual field and eye-movement amplitude in Buteo and other diurnal raptors, including the red-tailed hawk (DOI not confirmed because PMC blocked automated access; the PMC ID is PMC2943905).

authors: Hart NS
title: Microspectrophotometry of visual pigments and oil droplets in a marine bird, the wedge-tailed shearwater Puffinus pacificus: topographic variations in photoreceptor spectral characteristics
why: Method paper for retinal oil droplet and pigment topography in a seabird; background for how gull and tern rows could be interpreted.

authors: Cronin TW, Kinloch MR, Olsen GH
title: Head-bobbing behavior in walking whooping cranes (Grus americana) and sandhill cranes (Grus canadensis)
why: Measures the head-bob cycle in walking sandhill cranes: four-step pattern tied to stepping, gaze held still between thrusts, no bobbing when running.

authors: Cronin TW, Kinloch MR, Olsen GH
title: Head-bobbing behavior in foraging whooping cranes favors visual fixation
why: Foraging whooping crane keeps its head still at least half the time while walking; closest foraging data for the sandhill crane head-movement row.

authors: Necker R
title: Head-bobbing of walking birds
why: Review of which walking birds head-bob: cranes and herons bob, ducks and most gulls do not, crows hop or bob; settles the head-movement-while-walking row by group for sandhill crane, egret, ibis, mallard, ring-billed gull, crow.

authors: Fujita M, Kawakami K
title: Head-bobbing patterns, while walking, of Black-winged Stilts Himantopus himantopus and various herons
why: Bob-per-step patterns in eight heron species while walking; nearest measured group for the great egret.

authors: Montoyo YG, García M, Segovia Y
title: Light and electron microscopic studies on the retina of the booted eagle (Aquila pennata)
why: Cone types (red, green, blue and UV single cones) and oil droplets of an eagle; nearest eagle retina source for the bald eagle photoreceptor rows.

authors: Pecsics T, Csörgő T
title: Aspects of cranial adaptation in foot-propelled diving birds: foraging and visual fields of some piscivorous species
why: Estimates horizontal visual field of the anhinga itself, finding the narrowest binocular field of the species compared (cormorant and goosander wider).

authors: White CR, Day N, Butler PJ, Martin GR
title: Vision and foraging in cormorants: more like herons than hawks?
why: Behavioural underwater acuity in great cormorants is poor and prey is detectable only within about 1 m; closest acuity data for the anhinga.

authors: Strod T, Arad Z, Izhaki I, Katzir G
title: Cormorants keep their power: visual resolution in a pursuit-diving bird under amphibious and turbid conditions
why: Underwater visual resolution of a cormorant; background for anhinga amphibious vision.

authors: Moore BA, Tyrrell LP, Pita D, Bininda-Emonds ORP, Fernández-Juricic E
title: Does retinal configuration make the head and eyes of foveate birds move?
why: Dataset of 29 foveate North American and lab bird species (Appendix 1) with fovea position, ganglion-cell gradient, eye-movement degree and head-movement rate; open the appendix to see whether blue jay, cardinal, blackbird, crow, mockingbird are among them.

authors: Vasconcelos FTGR, Naman MJV, Hauzman E, Baron J, Ventura DF, Bonci DMO
title: LWS visual pigment in owls: spectral tuning inferred by genetics
why: LWS opsin tuning sites in five owls including a tropical screech owl (Megascops, same genus as the eastern screech owl); long-wave peak near 555 nm (DOI not on the page, MEDLINE ID 31706045).

authors: Vasconcelos FTGR
title: Estudo morfologico da retina e genetico do pigmento visual LWS de cinco especies de corujas e sua relacao com o ritmo circadiano (Master's dissertation, Universidade de Sao Paulo)
journal: Universidade de Sao Paulo, Biblioteca Digital de Teses
why: Retinal sections, cone immunohistochemistry and LWS sequences in five owls including Megascops choliba (genus of the eastern screech owl).
get: thesis (open access, PDF on the USP thesis page)

authors: Ödeen A, Hart NS, Håstad O
title: Assessing the use of genomic DNA as a predictor of the maximum absorbance wavelength of avian SWS1 opsin visual pigments
why: Checks SWS1 sequence against measured violet or UV pigments and tests the bobolink, an icterid; the sequence rule it validates is what lets blackbird and grackle rows be read from SWS1 data.

authors: Braekevelt CR
title: Retina photoreceptor fine structure (Anas platyrhynchos)
why: Rod:single cone:double cone ratio about 1:2:1 and oil droplet structure in the mallard retina itself (no DOI printed).

authors: Barber CL, Prescott NB, Jarvis JR, Le Sueur C, Perry GC, Wathes CM
title: Comparative study of the photopic spectral sensitivity of domestic ducks (Anas platyrhynchos domesticus), turkeys (Meleagris gallopavo gallopavo) and humans
why: Behavioural photopic spectral sensitivity from 326 to 694 nm in domestic (mallard-derived) ducks: peak 544 to 577 nm and UV-A is perceived.

authors: Yorzinski JL
title: Great-tailed grackles can independently direct their eyes toward different targets
why: Shows grackles (same genus as boat-tailed grackle) move left and right eyes independently toward separate targets; settles an eye-movement row for the boat-tailed grackle.

authors: Yorzinski JL
title: A songbird inhibits blinking behaviour in flight
why: Blink rate of great-tailed grackles through take-off, flight and landing (fewest blinks in flight); blinking row for the boat-tailed grackle by genus.

authors: Yorzinski JL, Argubright S
title: Wind increases blinking behavior in great-tailed grackles (Quiscalus mexicanus)
why: Grackles blink more often and longer in simulated wind; supports a blinking or weather row for the boat-tailed grackle by genus.

authors: Eaton MD, Benites P, Campillo L, Wilson RE, Sonsthagen SA
title: Gull plumages are, and are not, what they appear to human vision
why: Applies avian visual models to 13 Larus gull plumages; background on how a gull-type visual system is modelled, for the ring-billed gull ultraviolet row.

authors: Itahara A, Kano F
title: Gaze tracking of large-billed crows (Corvus macrorhynchos) in a motion capture system
why: Maps binocular width, optic axes and eye-movement extent in a crow (same genus as the American crow) and shows which part of the field crows use for moving versus still targets.

authors: Coli A, Stornelli MR, Barsotti G, Lenzi C, Bogi F, Giannessi E
title: Number and topographical distribution of retinal ganglion cells in diurnal and nocturnal raptors
why: Ganglion cell counts and topography in the common buzzard (Buteo, genus of the red-shouldered hawk) and tawny owl (Strix, genus of the barred owl).
get: open access (SciELO, International Journal of Morphology)

authors: Rahman ML, Aoyama M, Sugita S
title: Distribution and morphology of retinal ganglion cells of jungle crow (Corvus macrorhynchos) (conference abstract, 140th Annual Meeting of the Japanese Society of Veterinary Science)
journal: Japanese Society of Veterinary Science meeting abstract
why: About 3.6 million ganglion cells with peak density in area centralis and dorsotemporal retina in a crow; the full journal paper (about 2006, Anatomical Science International, title 'Number, distribution and size of retinal ganglion cells in the jungle crow') should be requested for the acuity row.
get: abstract only; find the 2006 journal article via library
